title: Money, Banking and Financial Institutions
objectives: Explain the three functions of money and why trust and acceptability matter
Read a simple bank balance sheet and compute equity, use and the capital ratio
Trace how fractional-reserve banking expands deposits and compute the money multiplier
Identify the roles of central banks, commercial banks, asset managers, insurers and clearing houses
motivation: Before you can price a swap or run a backtest you need a mental model of the plumbing: who holds the money, who creates it, who moves it between accounts, and who stands between two counterparties that do not trust each other. Every trade you will ever book is settled by this machinery, and every interest rate you will ever discount with is set somewhere inside it.

blocks.md: Money is whatever simultaneously serves three functions: a **medium of exchange** (people accept it in trade), a **store of value** (it holds purchasing power over time) and a **unit of account** (prices are quoted in it). Money is not the same as wealth, a portfolio of bonds is wealth but not money, and it is not the same as income, which is a flow per period. What makes an asset money is *acceptability*: everyone takes it because they expect everyone else to. That is why bank deposits count as money even though they are just claims on a bank, and why the system needs institutions that make those claims credible.

blocks.title: Money vs wealth vs income
blocks.md: A trader with \$250,000 in stocks, \$30,000 in a bank account and a \$95,000 salary has wealth of \$280,000, money of \$30,000 and income of \$95,000 per year. Confusing the three stock/flow distinctions is a classic modelling error: returns apply to stocks of wealth, not to income.

blocks.text: Banks: a balance sheet with a payment system attached

blocks.md: A commercial bank is easiest to understand as a balance sheet. It **borrows** from depositors (a liability: the bank owes them the money on demand) and **lends** or invests (an asset: loans, securities, reserves held at the central bank). The difference is **equity**, the owners' cushion. Here is a hypothetical small bank, in millions:

Equity $= 1{,}020 - 940 = 80$, so the capital ratio is $80 / 1{,}020 \approx 7.8\%$ and use is $1{,}020 / 80 = 12.75\times$. Use cuts both ways: if loans fall in value by 60, equity drops from 80 to 20, a 75% loss for owners from a 5.9% loss on assets. That asymmetry is why regulators cap use and why bank runs are dangerous: deposits are payable on demand while loans are not recoverable on demand (**maturity transformation**).

Banks do not keep all deposits in the vault; they keep a fraction as reserves and lend the rest. With a 10% reserve requirement, a new \$1,000 deposit lets the first bank lend \$900. That \$900 is spent and redeposited somewhere, letting the next bank lend \$810, and so on:

blocks.title: The deposit-creation chain at a 10% requirement
items: Round 2: that 900 is redeposited, reserves 90, new lending 810.
Round 3: lending 729, then 656.10, ... each round multiplies the previous by 0.9.

blocks.title: An upper bound, not a mechanical machine
blocks.md: The textbook multiplier is a ceiling. In reality banks lend when creditworthy demand and capital allow, customers hold some cash outside banks, and central banks supply reserves elastically. Modern banking systems create deposits by lending first and manage reserves afterwards, but the arithmetic above still explains why broad money is a multiple of base money.

items: **Central bank**: sets the policy rate, supplies reserves, is lender of last resort, regulates banks. Its rate decision reprices every asset you will ever model.
**Commercial banks**: take deposits, make loans, run the payment system.
**Investment banks**: underwrite securities (IPOs), advise on M&A, make markets.
**Asset managers and funds**: pool savers' money into portfolios, the demand side of most trading.
**Insurers and pension funds**: collect premiums/contributions today against payouts decades away, huge, long-horizon fixed-income investors.
**Clearing houses (CCPs)**: interpose themselves between buyers and sellers so a default by one member does not cascade.
**Dealers and market makers**: quote two-sided prices and hold inventory, the subject of later market lessons.

blocks.caption: A \$10,000 deposit at a 2% rate reaches about \$14,859 in 20 years. The deposit rate banks offer tracks the central bank's policy rate, which is why rate decisions move every saver's future balance.

blocks.md: Executing a trade and settling it are different events. **Clearing** confirms the trade and nets obligations; **settlement** actually transfers securities and cash. Settlement cycles are precise conventions: US equities and corporate bonds settle **T+1** (next business day) since May 2024; many European equity markets remain **T+2**; FX **spot** conventionally settles **T+2** (a trade on Monday value-dates on Wednesday). High-value interbank payments move through central-bank real-time gross settlement systems, which is ultimately where money is 'final'. For a quant developer this plumbing is not trivia: settlement dates, value dates and calendars appear in every position and PnL report.

The takeaway: finance is a network of balance sheets connected by payment rails. Interest rates coordinate the whole network, banks transform maturity, and clearing institutions recycle trust so strangers can trade. With that map in place, the next lesson quantifies the most important single idea in the building, that money has a time value.

guidedExercise.prompt: Using the balance sheet table in the lesson (assets: reserves 70, loans 900, securities 50; liabilities: deposits 900, wholesale debt 40), compute (a) equity, (b) the capital ratio as a percentage, and (c) use. Then state what happens to equity if loan values fall by 60.
hints: Equity is a residual: assets minus all liabilities.
Use is total assets divided by equity.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Equity $= 1{,}020 - (900 + 40) = 80$. (b) Capital ratio $= 80 / 1{,}020 = 7.84\%$. (c) Use $= 1{,}020 / 80 = 12.75\times$. After a 60 write-down, assets are 960, so equity $= 960 - 940 = 20$: a loss of 60 on assets wiped out 75% of equity, use at work.

independentExercise.prompt: A bank has deposits of 2,000, reserves of 250 and no other liabilities; its assets are reserves 250, securities 150 and loans 1,800. (a) Compute equity and the capital ratio. (b) Loans worth 90 are written off, what is the new equity? (c) With a 12.5% reserve requirement, what is the maximum total deposit money the system can support from a fresh 2,000 deposit, using the multiplier?
hints: Equity = assets, liabilities; the liability side is deposits only.

commonMistakes: Calling income 'money': money is a stock (a balance), income is a flow (per period).
Reading deposits as bank assets, deposits are what the bank *owes*, hence liabilities.
Treating the money multiplier as exact rather than an upper bound under simplifying assumptions.
Forgetting that equity absorbs losses first, so use multiplies both gains and losses.
realWorldApplication: Payment systems move trillions daily through central-bank rails; position keepers, settlement engines and margin calculators all encode the conventions (T+1, T+2, value dates) introduced here.
quantFinanceApplication: Every discount rate you will ever use descends from the policy rate the central bank sets, and every backtest implicitly assumes the settlement calendar, e.g. US equities T+1, actually worked as coded.
summary: Money is whatever is simultaneously a medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account; acceptability is the key property.
A bank borrows short (deposits) and lends long (loans): equity = assets, liabilities, and use amplifies asset losses into equity losses.
Fractional reserves support deposit creation bounded by the multiplier $1/\text{reserve ratio}$ - a ceiling, not an exact mechanism.
Central banks set the rate that reprices everything; clearing houses and settlement conventions (US equities T+1, FX spot T+2) move ownership after execution.

quiz.prompt: Which institution sets the policy rate that anchors other interest rates?
options: The asset manager with the largest fund
quiz.explanation: The central bank sets the policy rate at which it lends reserves to banks; every other rate in the economy is priced relative to that anchor.

quiz.prompt: With a 10% reserve requirement, what is the maximum total deposit money that can be supported by a new 1,000 deposit?
A bank has assets of 1,020 (reserves 70, loans 900, securities 50) and liabilities of 940 (deposits 900, debt 40). What is its equity?
quiz.explanation: Equity is the residual: $1{,}020 - 940 = 80$, giving a capital ratio of about 7.8%.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are financial *intermediaries* (they take positions between savers and borrowers)?
quiz.explanation: Banks, insurers and mutual funds all intermediate: they gather funds from one side and deploy them on the other. A clearing house is market infrastructure, it guarantees trades rather than channelling savings into investments.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences, why is a bank vulnerable to a run even when its loans are good?
quiz.modelAnswer: Because it borrows short-term demandable deposits and lends long-term illiquid loans, a sudden mass withdrawal forces it to sell illiquid assets at fire-sale prices, so even solvent banks can fail if depositors panic.
quiz.explanation: Maturity transformation creates liquidity risk: assets cannot be converted to cash fast enough to satisfy simultaneous withdrawals, so runs are self-fulfilling.

quiz.prompt: A US equity trade executes on Monday. Under the T+1 convention, when does it settle?
options: It settles only when the buyer chooses
quiz.explanation: T+1 means settlement on the first business day after the trade date (execution on Monday settles on Tuesday). FX spot uses T+2 by convention; European equities largely remain T+2.

flashcards.front: What are the three functions of money?
flashcards.back: Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account. Acceptability by others is what makes an asset money.
$1 / \text{reserve ratio}$. At a 10% requirement the multiplier is 10: 1,000 of new deposits can support up to 10,000 of total deposits.
Equity = assets, liabilities (the loss-absorbing residual). Use = assets / equity; at 12.75x use, a 5.9% asset loss wipes out equity.
Banks fund long-term illiquid loans with short-term demandable deposits, profitable in normal times, but the source of run risk.
